decision.reason: In the newly provided 24-page complete primary article (Waters et al., 2020), the authors test whether EIBI outcomes from a prior university-led multisite project (Cohen et al., 2006) could be replicated in a new, non-overlapping sample of 94 children with ASD (48 EIBI, 46 SAU, ages 18 to 75 months at onset) evaluated at baseline and annually for 3 years. Because the study collects and analyzes new empirical data to test the same hypothesis as Cohen et al. (2006), both the shipped row and blind target 0 accurately classify the record type as a replication.

Because these children were seen independently of the university-led project
that was involved in our previous study, the results indicate that favorable
outcomes can be sustained in a community setting. In addition, given the
wide age range of our sample, the results also support previous findings that
some children who are 4 to 6 years old at onset of EIBI can make substantial
gains in IQ, adaptive behavior, and school placement (Eikeseth et al., 2007).
The design of the present study did not allow for testing which factors made
it possible to maintain the effectiveness of EIBI outside of a university-led
project, but the setting did include features considered to promote sustainability
decision.reason: In Results (pp. 14-19) and Discussion (pp. 18-20), EIBI significantly outperformed SAU across all longitudinal linear mixed-model time-by-treatment interactions (IQ, NVIQ, VABS Composite, Communication, Daily Living, and Socialization), Year 3 WIAT achievement subtests, less restrictive school placements, and typical-range functioning on most measures. Under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1, the authors state an explicit original-specific overall replication verdict for Cohen et al. (2006), concluding that gains were comparable to their prior study and that favorable outcomes were sustained independently in the community setting.

In the current 2021 journal abstract, the authors explicitly state that the project was a systematic replication of a study conducted by Jones et al. using a demographically different sample of participants, testing the original NAART regression equation to predict WRAT4 reading grade-level classification. Both the shipped row and blind target 0 rightly code the record type as a replication.

corrected_value.title: Using the NAART to Estimate WRAT-4 Reading Grade Level in a Predominantly African American Sample

decision.reason: The current 2021 journal abstract identifies the target as 'a study conducted by Jones et al.' whose regression equation uses the NAART to predict WRAT4 reading grade-level classification. In the publisher-deposited reference list for this same 2021 journal article, entry CIT0011 provides the exact DOI 10.1080/09084282.2011.643966, which bibliography_metadata.json resolves to Jones, Proto, Musso, Barker, and Gouvier (2012), 'Using the NAART to Estimate WRAT-4 Reading Grade Level in a Predominantly African American Sample' (also corroborated as context by the related dissertation). Shipped row 780 is complete and exact.

Evaluated strictly from the available current 2021 journal evidence (abstract plus deposited references; journal full text remains unavailable), NAART error scores and WRAT4 WR raw scores were significantly correlated, predicted versus actual reading-level proportions at/above or below 4th and 5th grade did not significantly differ, and the authors explicitly conclude that the original Jones et al. (2012) regression equation accurately predicts reading level classification in the current sample (with raw-score distribution differences reflecting sample demographics rather than replication failure). Although the separate 2019/2020 dissertation context additionally reports Cohen's kappa (.00 at 4th grade, .78 at 5th grade), per the quality gate the thesis is a distinct work and context only and cannot transfer unverified body statistics or override the journal abstract's explicit overall successful verdict.
